flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at pictures of a crab, a woodlouse and a prawn's tail.
flow.say: A crab's armour cannot grow, so it has to break out of it. Can we invent armour that grows with you?
flow.kid: Read the problem. Armour that can grow. Look at how a woodlouse's back is made of plates.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Armour That Can Grow challenge. You design armour that can get bigger without being thrown away.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw at least two ideas before building.
flow.say: Draw two ideas first. Engineers always draw before they build.
flow.kid: Draw two ideas for armour that can grow.

ask.q: How will your armour get bigger?
good: I add a new piece at the end.

flow.do: Build the best idea from card, paper, tape and string. A grown-up cuts the card.
flow.say: Let's build it. Remember: it must cover the arm, bend at the elbow and grow 2 cm.
flow.kid: Build your armour. A grown-up helps with cutting.

flow.do: Measure around the armour. Slide a folded cloth underneath to make the arm 'grow'. Measure again. Check the elbow bends and look for gaps.
flow.say: Let's test it. Measure around. Now grow. Measure again. Any gaps? Does the elbow bend?
flow.kid: Measure around your armour. Slide a cloth under it. Measure again. Any gaps?

check.q: Why do overlapping plates let armour grow?
options: The plates get bigger by themselves
The plates can slide apart and still cover the gap
check.why: When the arm grows, overlapping plates slide apart a little but still overlap, so there is no gap. Picking 'get bigger by themselves' is the very thing a crab's armour cannot do. Nothing hard and dead can grow on its own.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what worked, what did not, and what they would change.
flow.say: What worked? What did not? What would you change next time?
flow.kid: What worked? What did not? What would you change?
flow.parent: There is no single right design. Praise designs that solved one problem well, and ask what a real animal might do instead.

challenges.title: Crawl Without Legs
challenges.problem: An earthworm crawls with no legs and no wheels. Make a model 'worm' that moves itself 30 cm across a table, without you pushing the worm directly.
constraints: You may pull a string or blow, but you may not push the worm with your fingers.
The worm must be at least 10 cm long.
Use only paper, straws, string, tape, rubber bands, cloth and things from home.
general: Make an inchworm. Fold a strip of paper into a zigzag. Pull a thread through it to squash it, then let go so it springs out. Tape a little sandpaper or a rubber band under the back end, so it grips while the front slides.
Copy the worm's bristles. Stick short pieces of a toothbrush or stiff paper fringe underneath, all leaning backwards. They slide forwards but catch backwards, so each push moves the worm one way.
Make a sock worm. Put a string through a sock, with a knot at the front. Pull and relax the string. Bunch and stretch, bunch and stretch.
creative: Scrunch the paper cover of a drinking straw down into a tight wiggly worm. Put it on a plate and add one drop of water. It stretches and wriggles. The water fills the paper, like liquid filling a worm's body.
Robot makers build soft robots that move like worms and octopus arms. Some are pumped full of air or liquid and then sealed, like the capped bottles in the Water Bones experiment.
Could your worm move along a tube or a hose, the way a worm moves through soil?
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own worm that moves in a new way. Draw it, build it, and measure how far it moves in 10 tries.
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. Earthworms crawl without legs by squeezing and stretching. Your job is to make a model worm that moves itself 30 cm.

setup.art: A zigzag-folded strip of paper with a thread running through it, lying on a table next to a ruler.
setup.caption: 1. Make a zigzag paper worm with a thread through it.

setup.art: A hand pulling the thread so the paper worm bunches up, with tiny backward-leaning paper bristles underneath.
setup.caption: 2. Pull and let go. Bristles underneath stop it sliding back.

setup.art: The paper worm at the 30 cm mark of a ruler, with a child cheering.
setup.caption: 3. Measure how far it goes.

flow.do: Watch an earthworm move, or watch the video in this unit. Remember how the water rose up the bottle neck when you squeezed it in Water Bones.
flow.say: A worm squeezes to stretch forward, then pulls up its back end. Tiny bristles stop it sliding backwards. Can we copy that?
flow.kid: A worm squeezes, stretches, grips and pulls. Can you copy that with paper?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Crawl Without Legs challenge. You build a model worm that moves without legs or wheels.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw two ideas before building.
flow.say: Draw two ideas. How will your worm move forward and not slide back?
flow.kid: Draw two ideas. How will your worm grip so it does not slide back?

flow.do: Build the best idea. Test it on a table next to a ruler.
flow.say: Let's build it and try it. Count how many pulls it takes to go 30 cm.
flow.kid: Build your worm. Try it. Count the pulls to go 30 cm.

check.q: Why do backward-leaning bristles help a model worm move forward?
options: They slide forward easily but catch when pushed backward
check.why: Backward-leaning bristles slide easily one way and dig in the other way. So each squeeze moves the worm forward and not back. Real earthworms have tiny bristles on every segment that work the same way. Picking 'they look like legs' is close, but bristles do not walk. They only grip.

flow.do: Try the straw-wrapper worm too. Then talk about which way worked best.
flow.say: Which worm went furthest? Which one moved most like a real worm? Why?
flow.kid: Which worm went furthest? Which one moved most like a real worm?
flow.parent: Any honest test is good. A worm that went 10 cm, with a clear reason why, is a great result.

opts: A chain of small bones down the middle of the back
quiz.why: A backbone is a chain of small bones called vertebrae. Picking 'a shell' mixes it up with snails and crabs, whose hard parts are outside.
A snake has a long backbone with hundreds of vertebrae, even though it has no legs. Picking the earthworm usually means a long, legless shape fooled you.

quiz.p: Out of every 100 named kinds of animal, about how many have no backbone?
quiz.why: About 95 out of 100 kinds of animal are invertebrates. Picking 5 swaps the numbers: animals with a backbone are the small group.

quiz.p: Remember the Backbone Census? You looked for animals in and around your home. Most families find more kinds without a backbone. Why?
opts: Small animals can live in many tiny places, like cracks, corners and plant pots
Small animals are not really animals
Only small animals live in flats
quiz.why: Small invertebrates fit into many more tiny homes than big animals do. Picking 'not really animals' is a common habit of thinking. Ants and flies are animals too.
quiz.context: Remember the Backbone Census? You looked for animals in the kitchen, the bathroom, at a window and on the balcony, and sorted them into animals with a backbone and without one.

quiz.p: How does an earthworm stay firm without bones?
opts: It is full of liquid squeezed tight by its muscles
It dries out in the sun
quiz.why: A worm has a water skeleton. Its muscles hold the liquid in tight, like a cap on a bottle full of water. Picking 'a shell inside' is a guess, but worms have no hard parts at all.

quiz.p: Which animal wears its skeleton on the outside, like armour?
quiz.why: A crab has an exoskeleton, a hard skeleton on the outside. Picking the jellyfish forgets that a jellyfish has no skeleton at all.

quiz.p: An animal has 6 legs and 3 body parts. What is it?
quiz.why: 6 legs and 3 body parts means an insect. Picking a spider is the most common mix-up. Spiders have 8 legs and 2 body parts.

quiz.p: Which of these is NOT an insect?
quiz.why: A spider is an arachnid, with 8 legs. Ants, mosquitoes and bees all have 6 legs.

quiz.p: Remember the Water Bones experiment? You pressed down on pairs of plastic bottles: open and empty, capped with air, and capped with water. You used books, then sat on the board, then squeezed the capped bottles by hand. When you sat on the board, the capped air bottles went down a little, but the capped water bottles hardly moved. Why?
opts: The water bottles were the lightest
Water cannot be squeezed into less space, and the caps held it in
The water bottles had air in them
The water bottles were a different colour
quiz.why: Air can be squeezed a little, so the air bottles gave. Water cannot be squeezed, and the caps kept it in, so it pushed back. That is how the liquid in a worm keeps it firm. Picking 'lightest' is wrong: the water bottles were the heaviest.
quiz.context: Remember the Water Bones experiment? You pressed down on pairs of plastic bottles: open and empty, capped with air, and capped with water. You used books, then sat on the board, then squeezed the capped bottles by hand.

quiz.p: In a fair test of the paper tubes, what should you keep the same?
opts: The paper size and kind, and the way you add books
quiz.why: In a fair test you change only one thing, the shape, and keep everything else the same. Picking 'only the shape' gets it backwards: the shape is the one thing you change.
quiz.context: Remember the Armour Tubes experiment? You stood three paper columns of one shape under a board, round tubes, square tubes or zigzags, and added books until they crumpled.

quiz.p: A starfish is a closer cousin of yours than of a snail. What does this tell us about the word 'invertebrate'?
opts: It is not one family. It just means every animal that is not a vertebrate
quiz.why: 'Invertebrate' groups animals by something they lack. It holds many separate branches. Picking 'starfish have backbones' is not right: they have no bones, but they share our branch of the family tree.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still argue about?
opts: Whether an ant's pain feels like ours
quiz.why: Leg counts, backbones and moulting are settled. Ants sense and react to harm, but nobody knows how to look at a feeling from the inside of another body. Picking the others mixes up open questions with things scientists have checked many times.

quiz.p: You find a snail after rain and want to look at it. What is the kind way?
opts: Keep it in a closed jar for a week
Hold it gently by its shell, watch it for a few minutes, put it back where you found it and wash your hands
Pull it out of its shell to see inside
Put salt on it to see what happens
quiz.why: Watch kindly, for a short time, and return the animal where you found it. Salt hurts snails badly, and a snail cannot leave its shell. Wash your hands, because snails can carry germs.

applications: Farmers and gardeners use earthworms to make compost, called vermicompost, from kitchen and farm waste.
Honeybees and many other insects pollinate crops like mangoes, mustard, apples and cotton.
Silk comes from the cocoons of silkworm moths. India is one of the biggest silk makers in the world.
Lac, used in bangles, polish and sealing wax, is made by tiny lac insects on trees in Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh.
Engineers copy spider silk to try to make strong, light threads.
Soft robots are built to move like worms and octopus arms, to squeeze into pipes or rubble.
A glowing green material from a jellyfish is used by scientists all over the world to light up cells and watch them.
Doctors once used leeches, and still sometimes do, to help blood flow in sewn-on fingers and ears.
Pearls are grown in oysters, and shells were once used as money in parts of India and Africa.
Prawns, crabs and mussels are important food, and fishing them feeds millions of families along India's coasts.
Scientists watch the insects in streams to check whether river water is clean.
Coral reefs protect coasts from waves and are home to a huge number of fish.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of animal without a backbone are there on Earth?
open_questions.why_open: Most of them have never been seen by scientists. Estimates go from a few million to many millions.

open_questions.q: Which group branched off the animal family tree first: sponges or comb jellies?
open_questions.why_open: Different studies of genes give different answers. Scientists are still arguing.

open_questions.q: What is it like to be an ant, a worm or a jellyfish?
open_questions.why_open: They sense, feel and react, and we can watch what they do. But nobody knows how to look at a feeling from the inside of another body.

open_questions.q: Why are there no giant insects on land today?
open_questions.why_open: Oxygen in the air, heavy armour and hungry birds may all play a part. Nobody knows which matters most.

open_questions.q: How can a starfish, with no brain, decide which way to go?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists are studying how its arms share messages, but they do not fully understand it yet.

open_questions.q: How does a tardigrade survive drying out, freezing and even space?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found special proteins that help, but they do not yet know the whole story.

open_questions.q: Why can some animals, like flatworms and starfish, regrow whole body parts, while we cannot?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists are finding some of the genes involved, but nobody knows the full answer.

maths.problem: In the Backbone Census, a family found 4 kinds of animal with a backbone and 9 kinds without. How many more kinds without a backbone did they find?
maths.explain: They found 9 kinds without a backbone and 4 kinds with one. 9 take away 4 is 5. So they found 5 more kinds of invertebrate. You can check: 4 + 5 = 9.
maths.context: Remember the Backbone Census? You looked for animals in and around your home, and sorted them into animals with a backbone and without one.

chart.title: Kinds of animal found in and around one flat

maths.why_maths: Saying 'more' is a start. Working out 'how many more' tells us how big the difference really is.

maths.problem: In the Leg Count Key, you looked at 3 ants and 2 spiders. An ant has 6 legs and a spider has 8. How many legs are there altogether?
maths.explain: 3 ants have 3 groups of 6 legs. 6 + 6 + 6 = 18. 2 spiders have 2 groups of 8 legs. 8 + 8 = 16. 18 + 16 = 34 legs altogether.
maths.context: Remember the Leg Count Key? You counted legs to sort small animals: 6 legs for an insect, 8 for a spider.
maths.why_maths: Every animal of a group has the same number of legs. So we can count in equal groups instead of counting every leg one by one.

maths.problem: In Water Bones, under 5 books the board sank 5 cm on the open bottles, half a centimetre on the capped air bottles and 0 cm on the capped water bottles. With a child sitting on it, it sank 1 cm on the capped air bottles and 0 cm on the capped water bottles. Put the three pairs in order from firmest to softest. Which pair is most like an earthworm, and why?
maths.answer: Capped water, then capped air, then open and empty. The capped water bottles are most like an earthworm.
maths.explain: The less the board sank, the firmer the pair. Under the books, the open bottles sank 5 cm, far more than the others. Half a centimetre is so small that it could be a mistake in reading the ruler. The sitting test is heavier, so it decides: 0 cm is less than 1 cm. So the order is capped water, capped air, open and empty. An earthworm is like the capped water bottles: liquid held in tight, which cannot be squeezed into less space.
maths.context: Remember the Water Bones experiment? You pressed down on pairs of plastic bottles: open and empty, capped with air, and capped with water. You used books, then sat on the board, then squeezed the capped bottles by hand.

chart.title: How far the board sank under 5 books

maths.why_maths: One test could not tell two pairs apart. Comparing the numbers from two tests shows which result to trust.

maths.problem: In the Many Small Suckers experiment, one sucker held 3 cups of rice. If every sucker held the same, how many cups should 4 suckers hold?
maths.explain: 4 suckers each holding 3 cups is 4 groups of 3. 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12. So 4 suckers should hold 12 cups. In the made-up results they held 11, a little less, because real suckers do not share the load perfectly.
maths.context: Remember the Many Small Suckers experiment? You hung a bag from rubber suckers on a tile and added cups of rice until they popped off.

chart.title: Cups of rice held before the suckers popped off

maths.why_maths: Multiplying tells us what to expect if every grip adds up perfectly. Comparing that with what really happened shows us something new.

maths.problem: The Bottle Wormery started on a Monday and lasts 14 days. You look on day 1, day 3, day 7, day 10 and day 14. How many days are there between the day 7 look and the day 14 look?
maths.explain: Day 14 take away day 7 is 7. So there are 7 days between the two looks. That is one whole week, so the last look is on a Monday too.
maths.context: Remember the Bottle Wormery? You made stripes of soil and sand in a bottle, added earthworms and looked at it over 14 days.
maths.why_maths: Slow changes need careful timing. Counting the days between looks helps us plan, and helps us say how fast the worms worked.

roots.context: We have been learning how animals without backbones hold their soft bodies in shape, and how they feel and decide. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Under the books, the open bottles squashed, but the capped bottles held firm. When you sat on them or squeezed them, the air bottles gave, but the water bottles hardly moved. Water cannot be squeezed into less space, so water shut in tight makes a body firm. An earthworm has no bones, only liquid held in by its muscles, and that is enough.
deep_truth.habit: We think being firm needs something hard inside, like bone or wood. An earthworm shows that liquid held in tight is enough.
deep_truth.evidence: In Water Bones, the open bottles squashed under the books, but the capped bottles held firm. Under a sitting child and a hard squeeze, the air bottles gave and the water bottles did not.

three.who_am_i: You hold your shape with bones inside. An earthworm holds its shape with liquid held in tight. Both of you feel the world you move through.
three.what_is_life: Life has found many ways to hold a soft body in shape: liquid held in, a shell, armour outside or bones inside.
three.what_is_this_world: Most of the animals on Earth are small and have no bones. They live under your feet, in the corners of your home and in the sea.

roots.thread: All animals come from soft animals that lived in the sea more than 550 million years ago. From those first soft bodies came worms, snails, insects, starfish, fish and you. Each line of animals found its own way to hold a soft body in shape: liquid held in, a shell, armour outside, or bones inside. So a worm, a crab and you are relatives who solved the same problem in different ways.

teachings.source: Acaranga Sutra, Book 1, Lecture 2, Lesson 3 (a Jain scripture, in Hermann Jacobi's translation)
teachings.teaching: All beings are fond of life. They like pleasure and dislike pain. To all, life is dear. This is why Jain monks walk softly and sweep the ground ahead of them, so as not to step on tiny creatures.
teachings.link: In this unit, crabs guarded hurt legs and an octopus stayed away from a place where it was hurt. The Jain teaching said long ago what these tests now show: small animals dislike pain.

teachings.source: Zhuangzi, chapter 2, the butterfly dream (a Chinese Taoist book)
teachings.teaching: Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly, happily flying about. When he woke up, he wondered: was he a man who had dreamed he was a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming it was a man?
teachings.link: We can watch what an ant or a butterfly does, but we cannot step inside its body to feel what it feels. Zhuangzi's dream asks the same question about what it is like to be a small creature.

science.text: All animals share one ancestor. Starfish, sea urchins and vertebrates are on one big branch of the family tree, so a starfish is a closer cousin of ours than a snail is.
In 2021, a review of more than 300 studies found strong evidence that crabs, lobsters, octopuses and squid feel pain. What an ant or a worm feels from the inside is still open.

other_view.view: They say we cannot yet measure a feeling from the outside. A worm pulling away from a sharp stick may be a reflex, like your knee jerking when a doctor taps it. So they would wait for better tests before saying a worm or an ant feels. That is an honest view, and many careful people hold it.

practice.title: Firm without bones
practice.say: Sit up tall. Hold your left arm out and let it go soft. With your right hand, gently press the soft part of your forearm. Now make a tight fist and press the same place again. It is hard now, because your muscles are squeezing. A worm's muscles squeeze its liquid in the same way, all along its body. Let the fist go soft again. Breathe in slowly, and out slowly, three times. Feel the squeeze and the softness, one after the other.
practice.kid: Let your arm go soft. Press it. Now make a tight fist. Press again. It feels hard. Your muscles squeezed. Breathe slowly three times.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1758 the Swedish scientist Carl Linnaeus sorted all animals into six groups. Four were animals with backbones: mammals, birds, amphibians and fish. Every other animal went into just two groups, 'insects' and 'worms'. So a crab, a spider and a butterfly were all 'insects'. A snail, an octopus and a starfish were all 'worms'. In 1793 a new natural history museum opened in Paris. Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, then 49 years old, was put in charge of the insects and worms. He studied their bodies closely and saw that they were not two kinds at all. Crabs breathe with gills and have ten legs. Spiders have eight legs and no feelers. His colleague Georges Cuvier showed that snails, clams and octopuses share one body plan, so he grouped them as molluscs. Lamarck gave all these animals one shared name, 'animals without backbones', or invertebrates. By 1801 he had split them into many separate classes. Scientists still use most of those groups today.
how_we_found_out.who: Carl Linnaeus, Jean-Baptiste Lamarck and Georges Cuvier
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Every animal without a backbone is either an insect or a worm. Lamarck and Cuvier looked closely at their bodies and found many different groups.
